summary: Describes best current practice on how devices, networks and services using IETF protocols should use existing standards to make emergency calls over IP networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A guide for how phones and networks should work together so that dialing for help reaches the right helpers when internet calls are used.

subtitle: The rulebook for phones, networks and call servers so an internet emergency call reaches the right local help, with a location attached.

tldr.problem: Emergency services are local, but an internet call can start from any network, so the call needs to be recognized as an emergency, carry a location and be steered to the right Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists numbered requirements for end devices (ED-), access networks (AN-), service providers (SP-) and intermediate devices (INT-): mark the call with a service URN, get a location, map it to a PSAP with LoST, and signal it with SIP.
tldr.outcome: Following the same requirements lets emergency calling interoperate globally. It is a Best Current Practice that complements RFC 6443, and RFC 7840 and RFC 7852 later updated it.

facts.label: Routing location time
facts.value: Recommended under 250 ms; typically under 100 ms

facts.label: Location update limit (by value)
facts.value: No more than one every 10 seconds

facts.label: Full test call interval
facts.value: About every 30 days, at a random interval

today: RFC 6881 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 181) and is updated by RFC 7840 and RFC 7852; read those together with it. It is not obsoleted by any other RFC.

sections.title: Scope and How Calls Are Placed
sections.content:
RFC 6881 describes how access networks, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) user agents, proxy servers and Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs) support emergency calling. It is designed to complement RFC 6443 in section headings, numbering and content, and the text says that understanding RFC 6443 is necessary to understand this document.

The requirements are tagged by who must meet them: ED- for end devices and applications, AN- for access networks (including enterprise networks), SP- for service providers, and INT- for intermediate devices such as a home router. Local regulations may affect whether the access network requirements apply.

The overview in Section 3 gives the whole flow. A call is recognized as an emergency by a unique service URN placed in the call setup signaling when an emergency dial string is detected. The caller obtains a location, either by measuring it (for example with GPS) or by asking the access network's Location Information Server (LIS). The location travels in the SIP signaling, and the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol maps it to PSAP URIs. The call arrives at the PSAP, or at an Emergency Services Routing Proxy that serves a group of PSAPs, with the location in the SIP INVITE.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a school with one emergency phone line that has to find the right fire station for any town in the world. Everyone in the chain, from the phone to the network to the call server, has a job to do so the call lands in the right place.

sections.title: Recognizing an Emergency Call
sections.content:
Which devices should support emergency calling? A device or application that implements SIP calling SHOULD support it (ED-1), and a service provider that supports a device expecting to place a call for help MUST facilitate it (SP-1). The RFC notes that regulations vary by jurisdiction, so it cannot say exactly when developers are required to support emergency calling.

Endpoints SHOULD recognize emergency dial strings, and proxies SHOULD do so if the endpoint does not. Emergency calls MUST be marked with a service URN in the Request-URI of the INVITE, and geographically local dial strings MUST be recognized. Dial strings SHOULD be learned from LoST, though they MAY be configured directly, and devices MUST be configurable with a home country so that home dial strings can be determined.

An endpoint that does not recognize a dial string SHOULD send it as a dial string URI as defined in RFC 4967. All sub-services of the sos service defined in RFC 5031 MUST be recognized. Devices SHOULD NOT offer one-button emergency call initiation (ED-10).
sections.plainLanguage: The phone has to notice when you dial the local emergency number and say clearly, with a special label, that this is an emergency call. A phone that does not notice can ask the call server to spot it.

sections.title: Getting and Carrying Location
sections.content:
Location comes in two forms, civic (such as postal addresses) and geospatial (coordinates). Endpoints, intermediate devices and service providers MUST handle both, and MUST NOT convert between the two forms before the call reaches the PSAP. Any location determination method MAY be used as long as its accuracy meets local requirements.

Endpoints SHOULD configure their own location from the access network. Devices MUST support both the DHCP location options and HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD), and the access network MUST support either DHCP location options or HELD. An endpoint SHOULD try all the location configuration protocols it supports, in any order or in parallel, and the first one that succeeds MUST be used. With HELD, the request MUST ask for emergencyRouting for routing, and a second request for emergencyDispatch is needed if a dispatch location is to be sent.

Access networks have duties too. Wired networks SHOULD support location configuration and, where possible, interior detail such as building, floor and room, which is recommended when spaces exceed approximately 650 square meters. If a network cannot determine the caller's location, it MUST supply a default location marked method=Default. A proxy MAY add location for an endpoint under conditions the RFC lists, and a proxy that has no better location MUST insert a default location.

Location is conveyed in SIP using the extension in RFC 6442. Location MUST be refreshed at the time of a call if it can be done quickly, and location determination is recommended to take no longer than 250 ms for routing, with typical response under 100 ms. If the location changes during a call, updates sent by value SHOULD be limited to one every 10 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers need to know where you are. Your phone can ask the building or network for its address, or measure it with GPS, and then tells the 911-style operator. If nobody knows exactly, the network gives its best guess, and says it is a guess.

sections.title: Finding the Right PSAP
sections.content:
Endpoints must first discover servers. They MUST support LIS discovery (RFC 5986) and LoST discovery (RFC 5223), MUST be able to learn their public IP address (for example with STUN), and MUST have a configurable default LoST server. If DHCP offers a LoST server, it MUST be tried first.

Endpoints that obtain their own location SHOULD ask LoST to map it to a PSAP URI, at boot time and whenever the location leaves the service boundary of an earlier answer or the answer's time-to-live expires. The result MUST be cached. At call time the endpoint MUST try to update its location and SHOULD try to update the mapping, falling back to cached values if a quick answer is not available. With no cached mapping, it signals the call without a Route header containing a PSAP URI.

Networks MUST be designed so at least one proxy on the outbound path recognizes calls whose Request-URI is a service URN in the sos tree. If there is no Route header, the proxy MUST perform the LoST mapping and insert a Route header with the PSAP URI. Proxies also MUST map calls from old user agents that did not mark the call, using the best location available, and a proxy whose mapping fails MUST provide a default mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: Your location goes to a big directory that says which dispatch center covers that spot. The phone remembers the answer in case the directory is slow later. If the phone cannot ask, a server on the way asks for it.

sections.title: SIP Signaling and TLS
sections.content:
The initial SIP message is an INVITE. For a user agent, the Request-URI and the To header SHOULD be a service URN in the sos tree, unless the device does not interpret local dial strings, in which case they MUST be a dial string URI with the dialed digits. The From header SHOULD carry the caller's address of record, a Route header SHOULD hold the PSAP URI from LoST, and the Contact header MUST be globally routable, for example a GRUU, so an immediate callback can reach the specific device.

A device that understands RFC 6442 and has its location MUST include it as location-by-value, location-by-reference or both. An SDP offer SHOULD be included and SHOULD offer G.711 for voice. A user agent that includes location-by-value MUST support multipart bodies, since SDP will likely be in the INVITE as well.

Proxies that interpret dial plans MUST look for the local emergency dial string and, when found, insert a Geolocation header (by reference, because proxies cannot insert bodies), insert Geolocation-Routing, map the location to a PSAP URI with LoST, add a Route header, and replace the Request-URI with the matching service URN. Proxies SHOULD NOT return a 424 error and SHOULD NOT obey a Geolocation-Routing value of no when they must query LoST, since emergency calls are always routed by location. An identity, such as a P-Asserted-Identity or Identity header, SHOULD be included.

TLS is the primary mechanism for securing emergency call signaling, and IPsec MAY be used instead for any hop. Either one MUST be used when attempting to signal an emergency call. If TLS setup is unavailable or fails, the call MUST be retried without TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The call is a message that says who is calling, what kind of help is needed, where they are, and how to call them back. Everything is wrapped in a lock when possible, but if the lock will not work, the call goes through anyway.

sections.title: Callbacks, Transfers and Disabled Features
sections.content:
Devices SHOULD have a globally routable URI in the Contact header that stays valid for several minutes after the call ends. Callbacks to that URI within 30 minutes of an emergency call must reach the device regardless of features such as do not disturb or call forwarding. Devices MUST also have a persistent address of record, in a P-Asserted-Identity or a signed From, for a later return call, although such a callback would not necessarily reach the original device.

During a call, a PSAP may transfer the caller by sending a REFER request in the dialog, and devices MUST react to it with the appropriate INVITE. Normal SIP procedures MUST be used to end the call.

User agents and proxies MUST disable features that would interrupt an ongoing emergency call, such as call waiting, call transfer, three-way calling, hold and outbound call blocking. They MUST also disable features that would block a callback, such as do not disturb and all kinds of call forwarding, and these SHOULD stay disabled for approximately 30 minutes after the call ends. Emergency dial strings SHOULD NOT be allowed in call forward numbers or speed dial lists. An endpoint can recognize a callback by remembering the PSAP's domain and starting a timer, with a suggested period of 5 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: After you hang up, the helpers might call you back, so your phone must not send them to voicemail. Features like call waiting or do-not-disturb are switched off for a while so nothing gets in the way.

sections.title: Media and Test Calls
sections.content:
Endpoints MUST send and receive media on RTP and use normal SIP offer/answer to agree on streams. G.711 A-law, and mu-law where intended for North America, MUST be supported, and if an endpoint cannot do G.711, a transcoder MUST be used so the offer reaching the PSAP contains it. Wideband codecs such as G.722 and AMR-WB are desirable in the offer. Silence suppression MUST NOT be used on emergency calls, because call takers sometimes learn from background sound what is happening. Endpoints with instant messaging MUST support RFC 3428 or RFC 4975, real-time text MUST follow RFC 4103, and video MUST support H.264.

Section 15 defines test calls. An INVITE to a service URN starting with test., such as urn:service:test.sos.fire, requests an automated test. A 200 (OK) means the address was recognized, 404 (not found) means it was not or that the PSAP does not support testing, and 486 (busy here) is returned if the test service is busy. The PSAP MAY return a text body naming itself, the service and the location it saw, and SHOULD accept a media loopback test.

User agents SHOULD run a full test after an IP address change not due to a reboot, and repeat a full test approximately every 30 days at a random interval. They MUST NOT place a test call immediately after booting.
sections.plainLanguage: Voices should sound the same everywhere, so everyone must understand one basic voice format. Phones can also place a practice call to check that everything works, but not all at the same moment.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 5069 and RFC 6280 for emergency calling security considerations. It suggests that TLS or IPsec be used hop by hop on a SIP call to protect location, identity and similar data.

It also suggests that if setting up the security fails, the call be retried without it. The stated reasoning is that it is more important to get an emergency call through than to protect the data, and in many jurisdictions privacy is explicitly waived for emergency calls. Placing a call without security may reveal user information, including location, but failing the call when security cannot be established is considered unacceptable.

Related cautions appear in the requirements: entities implementing DHCP for location SHOULD use DHCP message authentication to prevent spoofing, although providing credentials is difficult, and use of S/MIME with emergency calls is NOT RECOMMENDED because proxies need to read the location to route the call.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you would hang up if the privacy lock does not work. For emergencies, the rule is the opposite: help first, privacy second, because getting the call through matters most.
